# Maths S11 D05: Is this data numerical or categorical, discrete or continuous, nominal or ordinal? The arithmetic test, counted against measured, ordered against unordered labels, numbers that are only labels, and one question that gives either type depending on how it is asked (design)

Status: Revision 3 (25 Nov 2026): preflight and fact repairs (see the final section, "Revision 3 (root, 25 November 2026)"). Revision 1 (24 Nov 2026): first design, written to the maths visual standard (`../maths-visual-standard.md`), `math-s11-d01.md` to `d04.md` (Revision 1, this batch), the Year 12 design that recalls this video (`math-s12-b01.md`: "numerical variables (d05)"), the coherence audit and root's Standard rulings 1 to 99. Not voiced. Next: student learning review and Codex maths check, then voicing on the Google voice and a build on the studio kit to grade A.

Narration 5,509 characters by script (see "Narration length estimate"), 13 scene headings, about 497 s with holds (key notes fixed at 45 s). Nothing recorded; human listening pending.

Scope: fifth video of the Year 11 Data analysis strand, outline playlist order 65. One video for Standard 1 and Standard 2. Viewers arrive from d04's final frame. Pre-design pack: `../pre-design/maths-standard/math-s11-d05.md`. Route entry: `math-s11-d05` in `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`. Site lesson: `year11/data-analysis/lesson09.sa.html` (card 05, MC 1, 3, 5, drill 1, trap 01). Visual system: maths studio kit; the exam desk, phone, headphones, hotel facade, gym card and stopwatch plates (all existing); the record sheet, type tree, zoom ruler and switchboard coded.

Owner rules applied: as d01 (header strip "DATA ANALYSIS" only; one question; one stage at a time; plain meanings; two attempts with "Pause here to answer." and 10 s countdowns; brief feedback with one crossed slip; five key notes with a framed card; everyday anchors; no people, hands or faces; Australian spelling; no em dashes).

Syllabus content points (Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 11, Data analysis, "Data classification", common to Standard 1 and Standard 2), quoted from `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`:

- `cic8a0b6e9`: "Classify and describe variables as numerical or categorical"
- `ci038853db`: "Describe a numerical variable as discrete or continuous"
- `cic17a10b5`: "Describe a categorical variable as nominal or ordinal"
- `ci87535c02`: "Identify collections of data that can be described as numerical or categorical depending on responses"

Source: https://curriculum.nsw.edu.au/learning-areas/mathematics/mathematics-standard-11-12-2024/content/year-11/fa4de413b8

**Boundary:** starts from d04's final frame exactly (the exam desk `ma12-exam-desk-v1.png`, about 1,000 px wide, with the coded record sheet: columns "Sleep (h)", "Screens in bedroom", "Phone charges", "How rested?", "Gets to school"; first row "7.5 | 2 | bedroom | a little | bus" and four more rows; number cells tinted blue and word cells violet; chips "Numbers or words?", "Next: types of data" and "?"). Recalls d01 (the sleep buttons and the number box) and d04 (the record sheet) in grey chips. Teaches: variable; numerical and categorical; discrete and continuous; nominal and ordinal; numbers that are labels; the same question giving either type. Not taught: tables and graphs (d06, d07).

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the record sheet (d04's frame).** Five columns, five classifications. The sheet's columns peel off as cards and fall through the type tree, so every term lands on a variable students have already met in the investigation.
- **The arithmetic test first (site key tip).** "Does arithmetic on it make sense?" separates numerical from categorical before any other word is used. "Average of the postcodes" is the visual surprise.
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Variable ("something that can change from one person or thing to the next"); numerical ("the answers are numbers you count or measure, and arithmetic on them makes sense"); categorical ("the answers are groups or labels"); discrete ("counted: separate values with gaps between, often whole numbers"); continuous ("measured: any value in a range, as precise as your measuring allows"); nominal ("categories with no natural order"); ordinal ("categories with a natural order").
- **Continuous even when rounded.** Sleep is written to the nearest half hour, which looks like separate steps, but the time itself can be any value. A zoom ruler shows 7.5 h opening up into 7 h 32 min 10 s. Rounding changes how it's recorded, not what kind of variable it is.
- **"Depending on responses": two switchboard examples.** The sleep question asked with d01's buttons (ordinal categorical) or with a number box (continuous numerical); screens counted (0, 1, 2, 3: discrete numerical) or ticked as "none, one, two or more" (ordinal categorical). How the answers are collected decides the type of the data collected.
- **The type tree (recurring model).** Two questions: "Does arithmetic make sense?" Yes: numerical, then "counted or measured?" (discrete, continuous). No: categorical, then "Is there a natural order?" (ordinal, nominal). Reused in d07 when choosing graphs.
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Type tree** (scenes 2 to 4): variable cards fall from the record sheet and slide down the branches as the questions light, landing in four bins.
  2. **Zoom ruler** (scene 3): a ruler from 7 to 8 hours zooming in on 7.5 until minutes and seconds appear.
  3. **Switchboard** (scene 5): one question with two answer formats; flipping a switch reroutes the card to a different bin.
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and labels violet; answer green; mistake red. Here: numerical cards blue; categorical cards violet (as d04's record sheet tints).
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "arithmetic makes sense?", "average postcode?", "counted", "measured", "rounded, still continuous", "order?", "no order", "how you ask decides", "stars are labels". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The record sheet (1); the type tree, first split (2); the numerical branch and zoom ruler (3); the categorical branch (4); numbers that are labels and the switchboard (5); the record sheet classified (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the screen-time phone (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 6: the five columns labelled: "Sleep (h): numerical, continuous"; "Screens in bedroom: numerical, discrete"; "Phone charges: categorical, nominal"; "How rested?: categorical, ordinal"; "Gets to school: categorical, nominal" (framed green as a set).
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Count it or measure it: numerical. Name it: categorical." Key line: "Counted: discrete. Measured: continuous. Ordered labels: ordinal. Just names: nominal."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): discrete, continuous, nominal, ordinal; crossed "(d) numerical, discrete" (caption "stars are ordered labels"). A2 (pack question 2): "___ km" continuous numerical; ranges ordinal categorical; crossed "both numerical" (caption "how you ask decides").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. Digits as numerical (5); rounded as discrete (3); ratings as numerical (A1); one type per question (5, A2).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) some answers are amounts and some are labels, and only amounts can be added or averaged, so the arithmetic test sorts numerical from categorical (2); (2) counting gives separate values while measuring can give any value, and rounding only hides that, so measured data stay continuous (3); (3) some labels have a natural order and some don't, which decides what we can say about them, like "more rested" (4); (4) the type belongs to the answers collected, so changing the answer format changes the type (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (buttons and number box), d04 (the record sheet). Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** lesson09 classifications checked; MSY-37 (the "whole numbers" wording; the Year 12 labels; "depending on responses").
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d06a, grouping data).** Scene 12: board clear; the phone `ma12-phone-v1.png` (about 640 px tall) at the left with a coded screen-time screen: "Screen time yesterday" and "2 h 25 min" (48 px) with a small daily bar; at the right a scrolling list of 30 values in minutes (blue, 32 px, three columns): 70, 95, 110, 120, 125, 135, 140, 145, 150, 160, 165, 175, 180, 185, 195, 205, 215, 225, 235, 245, 255, 270, 280, 295, 305, 320, 345, 370, 395, 455; chips "30 different answers?", "Next: grouping data" and "?". d06a opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) 7.5 h = 7 h 30 min; the zoom shows a true value 7 h 32 min 10 s rounding to 7.5 h (nearest half hour).
  (b) 2 h 25 min = 145 min (one of the 30 class values; d06a's dataset T).
  (c) Postcode 2750 (Penrith) is used as a number only; any NSW postcode works. Codex confirms it is a real NSW postcode format.

Main question: *Five columns on one record sheet: which can we average, and which can we only count? Is this data numerical or categorical, discrete or continuous, nominal or ordinal?*
Entry knowledge (math-s11-d01, d04): the sleep question's two formats; the record sheet.
Stops after: four types by the tree; labels made of digits; the same question giving either type.
Handoff: math-s11-d06a: "Next: grouping data".

## Script and shots

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour roles (fixed): values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread amber; answer green; mistake red. Header strip "DATA ANALYSIS", with the mini investigation strip ("organise and display" lit). Scene headings in the hand font, 44 px.

teaching.task: # Maths S11 D05: Is this data numerical or categorical, discrete or continuous, nominal or ordinal? The arithmetic test, counted against measured, ordered against unordered labels, numbers that are only labels, and one question that gives either type depending on how it is asked (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: The first question sorts everything. Does arithmetic on the answers make sense? If the answers are numbers you count or measure, and adding or averaging them means something, the variable is numerical. Hours of sleep and screens in the bedroom are numerical. If the answers are groups or labels, the variable is categorical. Where the phone charges, how rested you feel, and how you get to school are all categorical. You can count how many students said bedroom, but you can't add bedroom to kitchen. Those counts are numbers, but the answers themselves aren't. That's the arithmetic test. Numerical variables split again. Is the number counted, or measured? Screens in the bedroom is counted. You can have two screens or three, but not two and a half, so the values are separate, with gaps between them. That's discrete. Hours of sleep is measured. Someone might sleep seven hours thirty-two minutes and ten seconds. Any value in a range is possible, limited only by how precisely you measure it. That's continuous. Time, distance, mass and temperature are all measured, so they're all continuous. Here's the trap. We wrote sleep to the nearest half hour, so the answers look like separate steps. But the sleep itself didn't come in steps. Rounding changes how a value is written, not what kind of variable it is. Sleep is still continuous. Categorical variables split too. Is there a natural order? How rested do you feel has answers not at all, a little, somewhat, quite, and very. They go in order, so the variable is ordinal. Where the phone charges, bedroom, kitchen, lounge or other, has no natural order. You could list them any way. That's nominal, which just means names. Getting to school, by bus or nearby, is nominal as well. The order matters for what you can say. With ordinal data, you can say one student is more rested than another. With nominal data, you can only say they're different, or count how many fall in each category.

teaching.openingDecision: Visual: opens on d04's final frame exactly. On "Here's our record sheet" the "Next" chips fade and the sheet enlarges (about 1,300 px wide). On "variable" chip "variable: changes from one student to the next". teaching.understandingCheck: Your turn. Classify each variable fully. A, the number of songs in a playlist. B, the time taken to download an app. C, a person's favourite streaming service. D, a hotel's star rating. Pause here to answer. Last one. A gym wants to know how far members travel to the gym. Write one way to ask that gives numerical data, and one way that gives categorical data. Classify each one fully. Pause here to answer.

scenes.teachingReason: The first question sorts everything. Does arithmetic on the answers make sense? scenes.teachingReason: Numerical variables split again. Is the number counted, or measured? Screens in the bedroom is counted. You can have two screens or three, but not two and a half, so the values are separate, with gaps between them. That's discrete. Hours of sleep is measured. Someone might sleep seven hours thirty-two minutes and ten seconds. Any value in a range is possible, limited only by how precisely you measure it. That's continuous. Time, distance, mass and temperature are all measured, so they're all continuous. Here's the trap. We wrote sleep to the nearest half hour, so the answers look like separate steps. But the sleep itself didn't come in steps. Rounding changes how a value is written, not what kind of variable it is. Sleep is still continuous.

scenes.teachingReason: Categorical variables split too. Is there a natural order? How rested do you feel has answers not at all, a little, somewhat, quite, and very. They go in order, so the variable is ordinal. Where the phone charges, bedroom, kitchen, lounge or other, has no natural order. You could list them any way. That's nominal, which just means names. Getting to school, by bus or nearby, is nominal as well. The order matters for what you can say. With ordinal data, you can say one student is more rested than another. With nominal data, you can only say they're different, or count how many fall in each category.

scenes.teachingReason: Two traps live at the edges. First, some numbers are really labels. A postcode like twenty-seven fifty is written in digits, but the average of two postcodes is nonsense. Jersey numbers are the same. They're categorical, nominal. Second, the same question can give either type, depending on how the answers are collected. Remember the sleep question's buttons? Under seven, seven to under eight, and so on. Collected that way, the answers are ordered groups, so the data are ordinal categorical. Ask people to type a number of hours instead, and the data are numerical and continuous. Screens work the same way. Count them, and you get discrete numerical data. Offer none, one, or two or more, and you get ordinal categories. How you ask decides the type of data you get.
